New model

Microsoft ships MAI Code 2

18 November 2026 · Reading time: 6 minutes

MAI Code 2 is a new coding model from Microsoft, built for everyday programming, and the company says it comes close to leading models at a much lower price.

Sapaude retells the story in its own words. The source is below. Publisher: Sapaude.

In three points

Three points, in this order: what the source shows, where that claim stops, and what to check next.

  1. At Ignite on November 17, 2026 Microsoft released MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash in GitHub Copilot. Microsoft says Code 2 reaches 98 percent of GPT-6.1 Sol and 96 percent of Claude Opus 5.5 on four coding benchmarks, at 40 percent and 5 percent of the cost.
  2. Microsoft says the models are not yet tuned for fundamental science or very long agentic work, the benchmarks are its selection, and the cost figures use a 50 percent promotional price.
  3. If you use GitHub Copilot, pick MAI Code 2 for one everyday task and compare the result and the speed with the model you usually run.

Microsoft now prices its own coder

On November 17, 2026, at its Ignite conference, Microsoft released two coding models it trained itself. MAI Code 2 is for everyday enterprise coding. MAI Code 2 Flash is for high-volume routine work. Axios, reporting the same day, puts the release in a longer story: Microsoft has relied on OpenAI and others for its most advanced models, and it is now showing specialized models of its own, competing on price.

Microsoft's post is explicit about the job it optimized for. Code 2 is meant for taking code to production, deep debugging, changes across files, reasoning over a repository and interface work, including changes a maintainer would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost. Flash is for explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes and quick iterations. Both are in GitHub Copilot. Flash is also in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry. The same day Microsoft announced a wider family, including models for cyber defense, images, live voice and transcription. This release note is about the coding pair. A derived model, MAI Work Flash, is the piece that serves Microsoft 365. Microsoft says it is about level with GPT-6 Luna on internal tests for Excel and PowerPoint.

Four benchmarks, a blind preference, a smaller sibling

The headline comparison is Microsoft's, dated November 17. Averaged over four coding benchmarks it chose because they match everyday work in GitHub Copilot, DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1, the company says MAI Code 2 reaches 98 percent of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40 percent of the cost, and 96 percent of Claude Opus 5.5 at 5 percent of the cost. All of those runs were at maximum reasoning effort. The footnotes say the MAI cost is shown at a 50 percent promotional price. Three of the benchmarks ran on Microsoft's own eval platform with the GitHub Copilot CLI and without subagents. FrontierCode scores and costs are from Artificial Analysis, with the MAI price still at the promotional rate.

A second Microsoft figure is about what people preferred to look at. In blind side-by-side tests of frontend work, reviewers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64 percent of the time. Microsoft says 258 annotators judged both appearance and function, across interfaces, games, charts, 3D scenes and SVG graphics. That is a preference on those tasks, not a claim that Code 2 wins coding in general. The comparison model there is GPT-6 Sol, not GPT-6.1 Sol.

Flash has its own line. Microsoft says it offers comparable performance to GPT-6 Luna at 65 percent of the cost and to Claude Haiku 5.5 at 20 percent of the cost, across three benchmarks for routine work: DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas. The Flash footnote also shows cost at the 50 percent promotional price. The Ignite overview uses the same 65 and 20 percent figures.

MAI Work Flash is the branch Microsoft describes for its own products, optimized from Code 2 Flash for Microsoft 365 and Fabric IQ. On Word, Microsoft says it performs similarly to GPT-6.1 Sol while staying significantly smaller, and uses about 42 percent fewer input tokens per call than GPT-6.1 Sol on five internal benchmarks. On Teams, the company says it beats GPT-6 Luna at tracking decisions, filling gaps and adapting custom instructions, with up to 28 percent fewer tokens on instruction following and tool calling. Those are internal tests. They explain why Microsoft cares. They are not a public leaderboard.

Hard problems stay out of scope

Microsoft states the limit in the post. The models are explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, such as fundamental science research and very long agentic work. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft's AI chief, told Axios the strategy is to put more capability into the same number of parameters. The trade-off Axios records, and that Microsoft's own sentence already states, is that a model tuned for everyday coding will not be as capable at advanced math or scientific research.

The price comparison needs the same caution. Axios notes that Microsoft's performance comparisons rely on selected benchmarks and that some pricing advantages reflect promotional discounts. That matches the footnotes: the eye-catching 40 percent and 5 percent are calculated with MAI at half off. Microsoft also says results vary by workload, configuration, reasoning effort and pricing assumptions. A number from November 17 at a promotional price is not a promise about the invoice later.

The wider family is context, not a second review. Microsoft used the same Ignite moment for other specialized models. Axios describes the push as cheaper models for particular tasks, while a general-purpose frontier model is still something Suleyman says the team is building, without a date.

One task you can already score

If GitHub Copilot is what you use, open the model picker and choose MAI Code 2 for a task you already understand: an explanation of a function, a targeted edit, or a routine fix. Compare the result and the speed with the model you usually leave on. Microsoft says Code 2 is built for that class of work.

Use Flash if the job is high volume and repetitive, and treat the limited Foundry preview as a separate door, not the default. Do not pick either model, on the strength of this post, for a very long run that has to keep going on its own, or for a problem Microsoft has said it has not tuned for. If the reason you switch is the price, read it as promotional until you see the rate on your own bill.

What you can do

If you use GitHub Copilot, pick MAI Code 2 in the model picker for one everyday task whose result you can judge, such as explaining a function or a routine fix, because Microsoft says the model is built for that work. Compare the result and the speed with your usual model, and remember the published cost gap is shown at a 50 percent promotional price.

In the app, the same story is also told shorter and in more detail, matched to your level.
